title: Body Systems of Plants and Animals
seo_title: Grade 4 Science: Body Systems of Plants and Animals Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_text: Plants have parts (roots, stems, leaves, flowers) that work together to take in water and make food. Animals, including humans, have body systems, such as the digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems, whose organs work together. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 4, Quarter 2: Living Things)
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 2: Living Things): parts of a plant, how water moves in plants, the digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Body parts work together in systems.
key_sub: Roots take in water; leaves make food.
body_html:
How to think about it

In plants, the roots take in water and minerals, the stem carries water up and holds the plant, and the leaves make food using sunlight. Flowers make seeds.

In animals, organs work together in systems. The digestive system breaks down food; the respiratory system takes in oxygen through the lungs; the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels) carries food and oxygen around the body.

Example

Which organ pumps blood?

In your chest

Answer: the heart

Example

Which plant part takes in water?

Under the ground

Answer: the roots

Common mistakes

  • Thinking plants get food from the soil.
  • Mixing up the lungs and the stomach.
  • Thinking the heart is in the stomach.

items.q: Joy stood a white carnation in a jar of water with green food coloring. Where will the green color appear after a day?

nowhere, the color stays in the jar
items.e: The colored water travels up the stem to the top of the plant.

items.q: Why does a plant droop (wilt) when it does not get enough water?
c: There is not enough water in the stem and leaves to keep them firm.
items.e: Water keeps plants firm.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Which does the water pass through first: the soil or the roots?
c: Water does not pass through either.
They happen at the same time.
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: Cut flowers in a vase stay fresh longer if you trim their stems. Why?

It stops the flowers growing roots.
items.e: Fresh tubes take up water.

items.q: A plant is pulled up and its roots are washed clean of soil. Why might it wilt after replanting?
c: Soil is not needed for water.
Many tiny root hairs were damaged, so it takes in less water.
Roots do not take in water.
items.e: Root hairs take in water.

items.e: Warm and sunny: more evaporation.

only at the bottom of the stem
items.e: The colored water travels up the stem to the top of the plant.

items.q: Why do leaves feel cooler than the air on a hot day?

items.e: Like sweat.

items.q: What does the stem do?
c: holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves
items.e: The stem is like a pipe.

items.q: Dennis stood a stick of celery with its leaves in a jar of water with purple food coloring. When the stem is cut across, what will Dennis see?
c: a purple stem all the way through, like paint

items.e: The tubes carry the water up the stem.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Where does it go after the soil?
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: A plant is kept in a dark cupboard for two weeks. What happens?
c: It turns pale and weak because it cannot make food.
items.e: Plants need light to make food.

items.q: Why are the tubes in a stem like drinking straws?
c: They carry water up from the bottom to the top.
items.e: A good model.

items.q: Jasmine stood a white carnation in a jar of water with red food coloring. Why does the color spread up the plant?
c: The plant takes up the colored water through tiny tubes in its stem.
The color floats up through the air.
items.e: The tubes carry water up from the bottom.

items.q: A drooping plant is watered. What happens a few hours later?
c: It stands up again as water reaches the stem and leaves.
items.e: Water makes the plant firm.

items.q: What path does air take into the lungs?
c: nose or mouth → windpipe (trachea) → bronchi → lungs
items.e: Air travels down the windpipe.

items.q: When you breathe out, what happens to the pressure inside the chest?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: On its way into the lungs, air passes through a bronchiole. Where does it go next?
